narrative:
The model that reviewed your law school application estimates a 64 percent chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In the university's eyes, you were more likely than not to struggle with the central hurdle of a legal career, and that risk led to the denial.

Three factors shaped this decision. The strongest was your third-year undergraduate class standing. You finished in the fourth decile, whereas accepted students typically reached nearly the sixth. This gap pushed the prediction firmly toward failure, suggesting that your later academic performance looked too weak for the demands of law school.

The second factor, your Law School Admission Test score, worked for you. At 38.5, it exceeded the accepted-student average of about 37.2, and the model treated it as evidence pointing toward passing. It was a real strength, but not enough to outweigh the concern above.

The third factor was your first-year class standing. You sat in the sixth decile, exactly equal to the accepted average, yet the model still counted it as a slight negative, nudging the risk upward rather than down. Its influence was small but noticeable.

To improve future applications, concentrate on the later part of your academic record. Retake demanding upper-level courses, complete a post-baccalaureate program with strong grades, or gain legal-related work experience that proves your readiness. Raising your LSAT score would also reinforce an area where you already stand out. The decision rested on these academic signals, not on your personal qualities, so addressing them directly is your clearest path forward.
